title: Parenting style quiz: authoritative, authoritarian, permissive or uninvolved? Free test — cv.cm
description: Free parenting style quiz: 14 questions about warmth and rules show whether you lean authoritative, authoritarian, permissive or uninvolved, with tips for each style. No sign-up.
lede: Firm or relaxed, warm or reserved? Answer 14 questions about everyday moments with your child to see which of the four classic parenting styles you lean toward.
about: In the 1960s psychologist Diana Baumrind described parenting styles by how parents balance warmth with control. Eleanor Maccoby and John Martin later framed it as two dimensions, responsiveness (warmth and support) and demandingness (rules and expectations), giving four styles: authoritative (warm and firm), authoritarian (firm but less warm), permissive (warm but few rules) and uninvolved (neither). In many studies, mostly from North America and Europe, children of authoritative parents tend to do well, but culture and the child's temperament matter too.

Seven questions ask about warmth and seven about rules and expectations, and your result shows where you landed on both. The questions were written for cv.cm from that model; they are not taken from any published parenting questionnaire. Your result is a snapshot of habits, not a grade, and every parent moves between styles on different days. If you don't have children yet, answer how you think you would act and read the result loosely.

faq.q: What are the four parenting styles?
faq.a: Authoritative (warm, with clear rules), authoritarian (strict rules, less warmth), permissive (warm, few rules) and uninvolved (little warmth or structure).
Research most often links the authoritative style, warm with clear limits, to good outcomes for children. But families and cultures differ, and small changes matter more than labels.
Many parents are. If one of your scores is close to the middle, you may mix two styles. Look at which of the two scores you'd like to move, and try one small change.
No. The quiz is scored in your browser and nothing is sent or stored.

items.q: Your child comes to you upset about something small. You usually…
options: Stop and listen, even if it seems minor
Tell them it's not a big deal and move on

items.q: Bedtimes and screen time in your home are…
options: Flexible; the kids decide most days
Clear limits that are usually kept

items.q: How often do you tell or show your child you love them?
options: Not often; they know it without being told
Every day, in words or hugs

items.q: Your child skips a chore you agreed on. You…
options: Follow through with the consequence you set
Let it go; it's not worth the fight

items.q: When your child does well at something, you…
options: Celebrate with them and ask how they did it
Note it briefly; it's what you expect
Mostly their business; I rarely check
Something I keep track of, and I expect real effort

items.q: Your child wants to tell you about their favorite game for 20 minutes. You…
options: Half-listen while doing other things
Ask questions and enjoy their excitement

items.q: Your child wants to go out with friends. You…
options: Ask where, with whom and when they'll be back
Let them go; they'll tell you if something's wrong

items.q: After you've been angry with your child, you…
options: Come back later to talk it through and make up
Let it pass without mentioning it again

items.q: The rules in your home are…
options: Few, and they change with my mood
Clear, and the kids know them

items.q: How well do you know your child's friends, worries and interests?
options: Not very well, honestly
Pretty well; they tell me a lot

items.q: Your child talks back rudely. You…
options: Set a calm limit right away
Ignore it to keep the peace

items.q: When your child is scared or sad, you…
options: Comfort them first, then help them cope
Tell them to toughen up

items.q: Your expectations for your child's behavior are…
options: Loose; kids will be kids
High for their age

authoritative.name: Authoritative: warm and firm
authoritative.body: You combine warmth with clear limits. You listen to your child, explain your rules and follow through. In much of the research this balance is linked with confident, self-reliant children. Keep explaining the why behind your rules, and as your child grows, give them a bigger say in setting them.

authoritarian.name: Authoritarian: firm, less warm
authoritarian.body: You set high standards and clear rules and expect them to be followed. Structure is a real gift to children, but without enough warmth they may obey out of fear and keep their feelings from you. Try adding more praise, more listening and more "here's why" to the rules you already have.

permissive.name: Permissive: warm, few rules
permissive.body: You are loving, accepting and close to your child, and you don't like conflict. That warmth is precious, but children also feel safer with clear, steady limits. Pick one or two rules that really matter, say them calmly and keep them, even when it's hard.

uninvolved.name: Uninvolved: hands-off
uninvolved.body: Right now you're giving your child a lot of freedom and not much warmth or structure. That often happens when parents are stretched thin by work, stress or their own struggles, and it's not a judgment of your love. Small steps help: ten minutes of undivided attention a day, and one or two clear routines. If you're feeling overwhelmed, it's worth talking to someone you trust or a family support service.
